A Pune software or web development company wins overseas clients from its website the same way it wins local ones, by making three things easy to find: proof that you have done similar work, a clear explanation of how you work across time zones, and a short enquiry form that captures what you need to quote and, later, to invoice. This article replaces an earlier piece that discussed the tax treatment of exported software services. Tax rules change and depend on each client's circumstances, so they belong with your chartered accountant, not in a marketing article, and we have removed that discussion on purpose. What a website can do is make the commercial side of an overseas project smooth: collect clean billing data at the start, set expectations on communication and contracts, and avoid the mistakes that make foreign buyers hesitate.

It is written for founders and marketing leads of agencies, software houses and freelancers in Pune and elsewhere in India who want more enquiries from clients in the US, UK, Europe, the Middle East or Australia. It covers the pages an international visitor looks for, how to show proof honestly, how to handle time zones and communication, what the enquiry form should collect, how to present pricing and currency, the data protection signals overseas buyers expect, and how to measure what works.

## What an Overseas Buyer Is Looking For

A buyer in another country has the same worries as a local one, plus a few more. They cannot visit your office. They may not know your city, your registration or how your work is regarded locally. They worry about time zone gaps, language, payment mechanics, contract enforceability and whether their data will be safe. Your website cannot answer every worry, but it can answer the first ones quickly, and a visitor who finds answers is more likely to write to you.

Think of the visit as a short checklist the buyer runs in their head:

1. **Is this a real company?** Legal name, address, contact details, registration information and named people.
2. **Have they done this before?** Specific work, ideally with results and permission to show it.
3. **Can we work together across time zones?** Working hours, response times, communication tools, meeting overlap.
4. **How do projects run and how are they billed?** Process, milestones, pricing model and payment terms.
5. **Is our data safe?** Privacy, security and confidentiality practices.
6. **How do I start?** A clear, low-friction way to make contact.

The rest of this guide is a build specification for those six answers.

## The Pages That Matter

### A home page that says who you serve

State in the first screen what you do, for whom and where you are based. "We build custom web applications and WordPress sites for businesses in the US and UK, from our team in Pune, India" is clear. A vague claim of "innovative digital solutions" is not. Naming your location is a strength, not something to hide: overseas buyers who search for Indian development partners are looking for exactly that.

### Service pages with the buyer's problem first

Each service page should open with the problem the client has ("our website is slow and loses leads") and move to how you solve it, what is included, typical timelines and how you work. Our guide on [headings, image alt text and semantic HTML](/blog/web-development-company-pune-image-alt-text-headings-semantic-html-seo-2026) explains how to structure those pages so both people and search engines can follow them.

### A page for each market you really serve

If you have genuine experience with clients in a particular country, a dedicated page for that market can make sense: for example, how you handle US business hours, the data-protection expectations of that region, or the currencies you invoice in. Do this only where you can say something specific. A page that merely repeats your home page with a country name swapped in is thin content, and Google's helpful-content guidance warns against writing for search engines instead of people ([Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)). Govindani Infotech's own [USA page](/usa) is an example of a market-specific page on our site.

### About, team and contact

Show real people with names, roles and photographs, the company's full legal name and registered address, and several ways to make contact, including email and a form. A phone number with the country code written in full helps overseas visitors. Do not hide the address, because it is among the first things a cautious buyer checks.

## Show Proof Honestly

Proof is the biggest factor in an overseas decision, and it is also where agencies most often overreach.

### Case studies

A good case study states the client's problem, what you built, how long it took and what changed afterwards. Only publish results you can support, such as before-and-after page speed measurements or a count of form submissions from analytics, and say how and when they were measured. Get written permission to name a client, and if a client wants to stay anonymous, describe them by sector and size instead. Do not invent testimonials, logos or figures. A case study with modest, true numbers is more credible than one that sounds too good.

### Reviews and ratings

If you display reviews from third-party platforms, link to the profile so a visitor can check them, and keep the reviews current. Our article on [testimonials and review schema](/blog/website-designer-pune-testimonials-reviews-section-review-schema-2026) explains how to mark them up without breaking Google's rules for structured data.

### Technical proof

Overseas buyers who are technical will look at your own site. Make sure it loads quickly on mobile, uses HTTPS and follows basic accessibility practice. Our guide to [HTTP security headers](/blog/web-development-company-pune-http-security-headers-hsts-csp-2026) lists easy technical signals of care.

### Work samples you can show

If client contracts forbid showing the work, build a small demonstration project of your own and publish a write-up of how you built it. It shows skill without breaching confidentiality.

## Time Zones and Communication

The question every overseas buyer asks, openly or privately, is "when can we talk?" Answer it on the page.

- **State your working hours in your time zone and the overlap with the client's.** For example, India Standard Time is UTC+5:30, so a Pune team working 10:00 to 19:00 IST overlaps with the UK morning and the evening of the US East Coast only in limited windows. Show the actual overlap you offer instead of "flexible hours", and confirm the exact offset for the dates you quote, since clock changes vary by country and year.
- **Show a time converter or a booking link** that displays slots in the visitor's local time. Most scheduling tools do this automatically.
- **Name your communication tools** and response expectations: email within one working day, a shared project channel, weekly calls. Only promise what the team will actually do.
- **Say who the client will talk to.** A named project manager is reassuring.

## The Enquiry Form: Capture What You Need to Quote and to Invoice

The enquiry form is where an interested visitor turns into a conversation, and it is also your first chance to collect clean data. Our article on [enquiry form design with fewer fields](/blog/web-development-company-pune-enquiry-form-design-fewer-fields-mobile-validation-2026) argues for asking little at first, and that holds for overseas enquiries too. A workable split is to collect a small set at first contact and a fuller set once the client is ready to proceed.

### At first contact (keep it short)

- Name and business email
- Company name and country
- What they want built, in a few lines
- Rough budget range and timeline (optional but helpful)
- How they found you (optional)

### At proposal or onboarding (a separate step)

Once a project is agreed, collect the details needed to contract and bill, using a secure onboarding form or portal and not email attachments:

- Legal entity name exactly as it should appear on documents
- Registered business address
- Billing contact name and email, and an accounts-payable address if separate
- Tax identification or registration number if the client has one, as relevant to their country
- Purchase order number, if their process requires one
- Preferred invoice currency and payment method

What you must put on an invoice, and how an overseas client should be treated for indirect tax, depends on the rules that apply to your business and the supply. Take this to your chartered accountant and refer to the official guidance on the GST portal and from the relevant authorities. We do not give tax advice here. The point for the website is simply that capturing these fields early, and checking them for format, saves days of back-and-forth later.

### Protect the data you collect

An enquiry form collects personal data, which you should treat carefully. Add a short privacy notice near the submit button, use HTTPS, store submissions securely and restrict who can read them. Our guide on [protecting contact forms from spam and bots](/blog/website-designer-pune-contact-form-spam-bot-protection-2026) covers keeping junk out without frustrating real visitors.

## Pricing and Currency on the Website

Overseas buyers compare prices, so the way you present them matters.

### Say how you price

Whether you work on fixed price, time and materials or a monthly retainer, explain it in plain language. Hiding the model makes buyers suspicious. If you publish price ranges, say what they include and exclude, and what a typical project needs. Where a figure is only illustrative, say so.

### Choose a display currency deliberately

Many agencies quote in US dollars, pounds or euros for clients in those regions. If you show prices in a foreign currency, label the currency clearly (USD, GBP, EUR) and say whether prices exclude local taxes where applicable. Exchange rates move, so avoid displaying a live conversion unless it comes from a reliable source and is clearly marked as an estimate.

### State your payment terms

Explain your normal terms in a short paragraph or a downloadable terms page: deposit and milestone structure, invoice timing and what happens if scope changes. Your contract carries the legal weight; the website simply sets expectations. Have your contract template reviewed by a lawyer who understands cross-border engagements, and be honest about it.

## Data Protection Signals for International Visitors

Clients in the European Union, the United Kingdom and some other regions are accustomed to asking about data protection. You do not need to claim certifications you do not hold, but you should be able to say, truthfully, how you handle data.

- **A privacy policy** that describes what the site collects and why. Our guide on [GDPR and India's data protection law when outsourcing software to Pune](/blog/gdpr-and-indian-data-protection-compliance-checklist-when-outsourcing-software-development) covers what buyers on both sides should consider.
- **A security overview** in plain language: access controls, backups, how client credentials are stored, whether you sign non-disclosure agreements. Do not claim compliance with a standard you have not been assessed against.
- **A cookie notice** that matches what your site actually does.

Obligations such as GDPR depend on the client's circumstances and the role you play, and are a matter for legal advice. The website should not claim more than your practices deliver.

## Make the Site Findable by Overseas Buyers

### Write in clear, plain English

Many overseas buyers are not searching with local jargon. Use terms they would use ("web development company India", "WordPress developer for hire", "custom software development") on pages where they match your actual services, and avoid stuffing them. Our article on [keyword research and search intent mapping](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-keyword-research-search-intent-mapping-2026) shows how to match pages to the questions people ask.

### Do you need hreflang?

If you have a single English site serving everyone, you generally do not need hreflang annotations, which Google describes as a way to tell it about localized versions of a page ([Google Search Central: localized versions](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions)). Use them only if you publish genuinely separate versions for different languages or regions.

### Structured data and consistency

Use organisation structured data with your legal name, address and contact details, consistent with the site footer and any public profiles. See our guide on [structured data and schema markup](/blog/web-development-company-pune-structured-data-schema-markup-2026).

### Be reachable where buyers look

Overseas buyers often check professional profiles and review platforms. Keep those profiles consistent with the website, and link to them from the About page.

## Measure What Works

Set up measurement before you start changing pages, so you can learn from the results.

- **Track enquiries by country**, using your analytics tool, so you know which markets your site actually reaches. Our article on [GA4 key events for forms, calls and WhatsApp](/blog/web-development-company-pune-ga4-key-events-form-call-whatsapp-lead-tracking-2026) explains how to set up form tracking.
- **Track source**: organic search, direct, referral, professional networks.
- **Track quality, not just quantity**: how many overseas enquiries turn into a proposal, and how many become projects. This lives in your CRM, not in analytics. Our article on [lead quality and offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026) explains how to connect the two.
- **Review monthly** and change one thing at a time.

## A Short Checklist

1. Home page states what you build, for whom, from where.
2. Legal name, address, team and contact details are visible.
3. At least two case studies with permission and honest results.
4. Working hours and time-zone overlap are stated, with a booking link.
5. Enquiry form is short; a second form collects billing details after agreement.
6. Pricing model and payment terms are explained.
7. Privacy policy and security overview are accurate.
8. Analytics track country, source and enquiry quality.
9. Tax and legal questions are directed to your accountant and lawyer, not answered by the website.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How can a Pune software company get clients from other countries through its website?
Show who you are, publish honest case studies, explain how you work across time zones, make the enquiry form short and answer common buyer concerns about pricing, contracts and data protection. A website supports these steps but does not replace direct conversations.

### What information should I collect from an overseas client before invoicing?
The legal entity name, registered address, billing contact, any tax or business registration number relevant to their country, a purchase order number if needed and the preferred currency. Confirm tax and invoice requirements with your chartered accountant.

### Do I need a separate website for each country?
Usually not. One clear English site is enough for most services. Create market-specific pages only where you have something specific to say, and use hreflang only for genuinely separate regional or language versions.

### Should I display prices in foreign currency?
You can, if you label the currency clearly, explain what the price includes and avoid implying a live exchange rate. Many agencies instead publish typical ranges and quote exact amounts per project.

### What should I say about time zones on my site?
State your working hours, the overlap with your client's working day and how quickly you reply, and offer a booking tool that shows slots in the visitor's local time. Only promise availability that your team can deliver.
